chapters.title: Chapter 2: Cyclical, Defensive, and Growth Sectors

lessons.title: Rates, Inflation, Crude, and the Rupee: Mapping Macro Drivers to Sectors

body.text: Every macro headline is good news for some sectors and bad news for others. A rate hike, a crude oil spike, or a falling rupee never hits 'the market' evenly. If you can map each of the four big macro drivers to the sectors they help and hurt, you can read a news alert and know within seconds which of your holdings just got more or less risky.

children.text: The first three lessons of this chapter dealt with the economic cycle as a whole. In reality, the cycle reaches companies through specific channels. For Indian investors, four matter most: interest rates set by the RBI, inflation in input costs, the price of crude oil, and the rupee's exchange rate against the US dollar. This lesson builds a sector map for each one, then tests it against 2022, the year all four moved at once.

Rates reach sectors through three channels. First, customer financing: most homes, cars, two-wheelers, and trucks are bought on loans, so higher EMIs reduce demand. Second, company borrowing: debt-heavy businesses such as infrastructure developers, power producers, and NBFCs pay more interest. Third, valuation: higher rates raise the return investors demand, which hurts stocks priced on earnings far in the future, typically high-growth, high P/E names. Banks are the interesting exception, covered in the box below.

body.title: Why rate hikes can help bank margins, at least at first

children.text: Since October 2019, the RBI has required banks to link new floating-rate retail and MSME loans to an external benchmark, most commonly the repo rate. When the RBI hikes, these loans reprice upward quickly. Deposits, especially fixed deposits, reprice more slowly as old FDs mature. For a few quarters, loan yields rise faster than deposit costs, and net interest margins widen. When rates are cut, the same lag works in reverse and margins compress. Banks with a large share of low-cost current and savings account deposits benefit most from hikes.

markDefs.definition: A company's ability to raise its selling prices to cover higher costs without losing significant sales volume. Strong brands, market leadership, and few substitutes create pricing power.

children.text: Inflation is not one number for companies. What matters is whether their input costs are rising faster than the prices they can charge. Commodity producers such as metal and mining companies usually benefit, because they sell the very thing whose price is rising. Companies that buy those commodities as raw materials, such as FMCG, paints, autos, and consumer durables, get squeezed unless they have
. Even strong brands pass on costs with a lag of one or two quarters, so gross margins typically dip first and recover later.

India imports the large majority of the crude oil it consumes, commonly estimated at over 85%, so crude is one of the most important prices for the Indian market. Crude feeds directly into aviation turbine fuel for airlines, into paint raw materials and packaging made from petrochemicals, into synthetic rubber and carbon black for tyre makers, and into freight costs for almost everyone. Upstream producers such as ONGC and Oil India earn more when crude rises, though government levies can cap that gain. Oil marketing companies such as IOC, BPCL, and HPCL are hurt when crude rises but retail petrol and diesel prices are held steady.

When the rupee weakens against the dollar, every dollar a company earns converts into more rupees. That helps exporters: IT services companies that bill clients in dollars, pharma companies selling generics in the US, and specialty chemical exporters. It hurts importers, whose dollar costs now take more rupees to pay: oil marketing companies, electronics assemblers, airlines paying aircraft leases in dollars, and any company carrying unhedged foreign currency debt.

body.caption: For a company billing entirely in dollars, rupee depreciation lifts rupee revenue almost one for one, before hedging

body.title: The Rupee's Gift to an IT Exporter
body.prompt: An IT services company earns $1 billion of revenue in a year, all billed in US dollars. Its dollar revenue stays exactly the same next year, but the average USD/INR rate moves from 83 to 86. By what percentage does its rupee revenue increase? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Rupee revenue moves from $1 billion × 83 = ₹8,300 crore to $1 billion × 86 = ₹8,600 crore. Increase = 300 ÷ 8,300 = 3.6%, with zero growth in the underlying business. Since most IT costs are salaries paid in rupees, much of this gain can flow to margins. In practice, companies hedge part of their dollar revenue, which smooths both gains and losses.

body.text: Treat this map as a first draft, not a rulebook. Hedging, pricing power, debt levels, and the export share of revenue all change how strongly a specific company reacts. Two companies in the same sector can sit in different cells.

body.title: Read the Headline
body.question: Headline: 'Brent crude jumps 25% in a month; rupee slides to a record low against the dollar.' Which sector is hit hardest by both parts of this headline at once?
body.explanation: Airlines take a double hit: fuel is one of their largest costs and is linked to crude, and many of their costs, including aircraft leases and fuel purchases, are effectively priced in dollars. IT services and pharma exporters benefit from the weaker rupee. Upstream producers benefit from higher crude.

body.title: How the 2022 Macro Shocks Moved Through Sectors

events.title: Crude spikes
events.description: Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent Brent crude above $120. Paint, tyre, and airline stocks came under pressure as markets priced in a raw material and fuel cost squeeze.

events.title: RBI begins hiking
events.description: An unscheduled 40 basis point hike took the repo rate from 4.00% to 4.40%, the first increase in nearly four years, as CPI inflation stayed well above the RBI's tolerance band.

events.title: Oil marketing companies post losses
events.description: With retail petrol and diesel prices held unchanged for long stretches while crude stayed high, IOC, BPCL, and HPCL reported losses for the quarter.

events.title: Windfall tax and a weak rupee
events.description: The government introduced a special additional excise duty on domestic crude production, limiting upstream producers' gains from high prices. The rupee crossed 80 against the dollar in the same month.

events.title: Banks shine, rate-sensitive growth stocks lag
events.description: Bank margins widened as floating-rate loans repriced, and falling bad loans boosted profits, especially at public sector banks. Richly valued growth stocks, including many new-age tech listings, saw their valuations compress sharply as rates rose.

body.title: The Paint Company Margin Squeeze
body.scenario: A leading Indian paint company has raw material costs equal to 55% of revenue, and a large share of those raw materials are linked to crude oil derivatives. Crude prices rise sharply and the rupee weakens in the same quarter. The company has strong brands and has historically raised prices during cost spikes.
body.prompt: What would you expect to see in its next two to three quarterly results, and what would you track to judge whether the stock's reaction is overdone?
body.modelAnswer: Expect gross margins to fall first, because raw material costs rise immediately while price increases are announced in steps and take time to reach dealers and customers. Crude and the weak rupee both raise the cost of imported and crude-linked inputs. If the brand is strong, the company should announce one or more price hikes, and gross margins should start recovering within a few quarters, though volume growth may slow if prices rise too much. Track: gross margin trend quarter on quarter, the size and timing of price increases mentioned in management commentary, volume growth versus value growth, and the direction of crude and USD/INR. If crude stabilises and price hikes stick, the margin dip may prove temporary, and a sharp fall in the stock could be overdone. If competition prevents price hikes, the damage is more lasting.

body.text: Markets move on expectations, not on the data release. By the time a rate hike or crude spike is confirmed, sector stocks have often already moved. Use the map to understand your exposure, not to trade the headline after everyone else has read it.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: A weaker rupee generally helps sectors that earn revenue in dollars, such as IT services and pharma ___.
body.explanation: Dollar revenue converts into more rupees when the rupee weakens, while costs such as salaries stay in rupees, which supports margins.

body.title: Build a Macro Map for Your Own Portfolio
steps: List your ten largest holdings, including the top sector weights of your equity mutual funds
For each one, mark its likely reaction to rising rates, rising input costs, rising crude, and a weaker rupee: positive, negative, or neutral
Check whether most of your portfolio carries the same sign for any single driver; that is your hidden macro bet
For the biggest exposures, read the latest annual report for hedging policy, export share of revenue, and debt levels to refine your marks
Note which data releases matter most for you: RBI policy dates, monthly CPI, Brent crude, or USD/INR
Revisit the map when you add a new holding, not every time a headline breaks

points: Four macro drivers matter most for Indian sectors: interest rates, input cost inflation, crude oil, and the rupee
Rate hikes hurt loan-dependent demand (real estate, autos), debt-heavy businesses, and high-valuation growth stocks, but can widen bank margins in the short run
Input inflation helps commodity producers and squeezes buyers of commodities unless they have pricing power, which usually works with a lag
India imports most of its crude, so a crude spike hurts airlines, paints, tyres, and oil marketing companies while helping upstream producers
A weaker rupee helps dollar earners like IT services and pharma exporters and hurts importers and companies with unhedged foreign debt
In 2022, rate hikes, a crude spike, and a record-weak rupee arrived together, and sector outcomes followed the map closely

body.text: Macro data points are approximate and quoted for educational purposes; refer to the RBI, PPAC, and official exchange rate sources for exact figures. The sensitivity map is a simplified framework and individual companies can behave differently. Nothing here is investment advice.
